opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think robotics is going to lag digital applications, and I think it's going to lag by quite a bit, actually. The basic reason is that atoms are just a lot harder than bits. In the digital world you can copy-paste things, you can iterate extremely quickly, you can deploy a new model to millions of people overnight, and if something goes wrong you roll it back. In the physical world, every single unit costs money to manufacture, you have to deal with supply chains, with hardware failures, with maintenance, with safety. So there's a lot more friction, and that friction slows down the whole loop of build, deploy, learn, improve.

That said, I'm actually quite bullish on robotics over the long term. A lot of the same technology transfers. The transformer doesn't really care whether it's predicting the next token of text or the next action of a robot arm. So a lot of the progress we're seeing in the digital space, in representation learning, in large pretrained models, in vision, does carry over. In some sense the "brain" side of the problem is getting solved in the digital domain first, and then robotics gets to inherit it.

I also tend to think about it a bit like what I saw with self-driving at Tesla. Self-driving is really the first robotics application at scale, and it took a very long time from the first impressive demos to something that actually works across the long tail of situations. I'd expect general-purpose robotics, humanoids and so on, to follow a similar arc: very impressive demos fairly early, and then a long, grinding march through the long tail before it's truly deployed broadly. So the digital transformation will happen first and faster, and the physical one will come after it, more slowly, but I think it will ultimately be just as large, if not larger, because the physical economy is enormous.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts that robotics will lag digital applications and says the digital transformation will happen first and faster.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that AI will make inefficient digital activities roughly a hundred times more efficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that robotics is going to lag the digital stuff by a meaningful amount, and I think people sometimes underestimate how large that gap is going to be. The reason is basically that the digital world has this property where the cost of iteration is near zero. You can run a million experiments overnight, the data is already there on the internet, you can copy-paste a model to a billion devices instantly, and if something breaks, nothing physically breaks. All of the fundamental ingredients that made the LLM revolution happen so fast are things that the physical world just doesn't give you for free.

With robots, every one of those gets harder. The data isn't lying around. You have to go collect it, and collecting it means a physical robot doing a physical thing in real time, which is slow and expensive and doesn't parallelize the way GPUs do. Then there's the hardware itself. Actuators, hands, batteries, sensors, all of it is still fairly immature, and hardware improves on a much slower exponential than software does. You can't just scale a hand by adding more parameters. And then deployment is a whole separate problem, because a robot that's right 99 percent of the time is a robot that drops your dishes once a day, and the tolerance for failure in the physical world is much, much lower than for a chatbot that occasionally says something dumb.

That said, I'm actually quite optimistic in the long run, because the transfer from the digital side is real. What's happened is that the neural net side of robotics, the perception, the understanding of the scene, the high-level reasoning about what to do, that part has been massively de-risked by the progress in vision and language models. When I was at Tesla working on Autopilot, a huge amount of the difficulty was in getting the network to actually understand what it's looking at, and that is dramatically easier today. So the brain is coming along for the ride, and what remains is more the body and the data flywheel.

My rough mental model is that it looks less like a single moment and more like a gradual march of autonomy, similar to what we saw in self-driving. Self-driving was supposedly two years away for about a decade, and now it's actually here in a few cities, but it took a long grind of nines of reliability to get there. I think general robotics follows the same shape. You'll see it show up first in constrained settings, warehouses, factories, places where the environment is controlled and the economics clearly work, and it'll creep outward from there. The humanoid form factor I think is a good bet in the long term because the world is built for humans, but I'd expect the digital agents that do your work on a computer to be transforming the economy years before a robot is reliably folding your laundry.

So, same underlying technology, very different time constants. Software eats the world fast, and then atoms catch up slowly.

r001.rationale: The response says collecting physical robot data is slow and expensive and that hardware is immature, but it does not communicate a need for large capital investments.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts robotics will lag digital applications by a meaningful amount and says digital agents will transform the economy years before reliable household robots.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that AI will make currently inefficient digital activities roughly a hundred times more efficient.

astra-6.text:
I think digital applications are going to move much faster. In the digital world, you can run lots of experiments in parallel, collect data relatively cheaply, and deploy an improvement almost instantly. With robotics, you have this physical loop: you need hardware, it breaks, you have to reset the environment, and collecting experience takes actual time. You can’t just spin up a million robots as easily as you can spin up a million copies of a program.

So I’m very excited about robotics, but I expect it to lag. A lot of the intelligence will come from progress in digital systems, and that should help tremendously. But having a model that understands what needs to happen is different from having a reliable machine that can actually do it in someone’s kitchen. That last part has a lot of engineering in it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think digital applications are going to move much faster. In the digital world, you can run experiments in parallel, collect feedback, and ship an improvement to everyone almost instantly. With robotics, you have this physical bottleneck. You need the hardware, you need to collect data, things break, and every experiment takes actual wall-clock time. You can’t just spin up another thousand robots the way you spin up another thousand processes.

But I’m optimistic that a lot of the intelligence will transfer. Understanding what’s happening in a scene, following instructions, planning—those are capabilities we’re developing in the digital domain that should help robots too. The harder part is connecting that intelligence to reliable action in the physical world.

So I’d expect a gap. We’ll have very capable digital assistants while robots still look surprisingly limited. And then robotics will improve as we figure out the data collection and deployment loop. It’s a different pace of progress because you have to contend with the physical world.
